axes.model_access:
**The integration surface is "300+ separate integration packages", not a unified gateway.**

- The official integrations page calls them all "community integrations"
- That is, most are community-maintained, not hand-fed by the vendor one by one

"There are **over 300 LlamaIndex integration packages** that work seamlessly
with core, allowing you to build with your **preferred LLM, embedding, and vector store
providers**."

The namespace rule is easy to remember:

- With `.core` (`from llama_index.core.xxx`) = core
- Without it (`from llama_index.xxx.yyy`) = an integration package

New integrations go through maintainer review.

**The README states**: "some integrations may be declined".

**Unknown: the official docs publish no quality tiering or maintenance-activity grading for the integration packages.**
(**Checked** — README and the integrations page.)
axes.runtime:
**The OSS form is a pure library with two install tiers; hosted execution lives on the commercial-platform side.**

**Two install tiers** (README Getting Started):

- **Starter** — `llama-index` (PyPI): core plus a bundle of common integrations
- **Customized** — `llama-index-core`: core only, then pick packages from the integrations page

**The framework itself is a library you import.** The way in is to connect with your outer application framework,
which is also **the fourth item of the README's Proposed Solution**:

"integrations with your outer application framework"

The vendor has a separate hosted/deployment path. LlamaAgents' `llamactl` CLI can be used like this:

**Official wording**: "serve locally, and deploy to LlamaCloud or export for self-hosting"

LlamaCloud also offers hosted Indexing.

- **Hosting is the LlamaCloud / LlamaAgents layer (commercial)**
- It is not a run form that ships with the OSS framework
axes.local_files:
**It reads local files to build indexes, not to give an agent a workspace.**

The official `SimpleDirectoryReader` docs put it plainly:

"the simplest way to load data from local files into LlamaIndex"

Parameters you can pass:

- `input_dir`, `recursive=True`
- `exclude`, `required_exts`, `num_files_limit`
- Remote file systems go through `fsspec` (S3, GDrive, etc.)

**Indexes live in memory by default.** Two official example actions:

- Persist: `index.storage_context.persist()` writes to `./storage`
- Reload: `load_index_from_storage`

**This site records this axis from the "index layer" perspective.**

It is not an "agent workspace" file system.
It is local file reading at the "data-source ingestion + indexing" layer.

It reads disk to turn documents into retrievable indexes.
That is not the same thing as Deep Agents' "agent editing files in a workspace".
axes.background:
**There is no hosted execution that "keeps running after shutdown".**
But orchestration (Workflows) really is still in the OSS.

**One spot is easy to misread from the README.** The README lists Workflows under the LlamaParse platform's
Agents section, while the official framework docs are explicit:

"llama-index-core comes with a stable version of Workflows included"

So orchestration has not been moved out of the OSS. Two entry points:

- Import path `llama_index.core.workflow`
- Also standalone: `pip install llama-index-workflows`

**Background execution is the missing item.** The official framework docs offer no hosted runtime for
"keep-running-after-shutdown"; you run the process yourself. For hosting, go through LlamaAgents / `llamactl`:

"deploy them to LlamaCloud or your own infrastructure"

and that is the platform side.
axes.tools:
**Two things at the tool layer: community ToolSpecs, plus one official MCP connector package.**

The official tools docs give `FunctionTool`.
There is also `QueryEngineTool`.
Plus **"Community contributed ToolSpecs"**.

Handling "a tool returns an oversized output" is what Utility Tools do:

- `OnDemandLoaderTool`
- `LoadAndSearchToolSpec`

**MCP is officially supported, as a separate package.** **Docs wording**: "LlamaIndex provides robust support for consuming MCP servers through the `llama-index-tools-mcp` package"

Its MCP surface:

- All three transports supported: SSE / Streamable HTTP / stdio
- A Workflow can be re-published as an MCP server
- The vendor also hosts `mcp.llamaindex.ai` (a docs-retrieval / LlamaParse MCP service)
axes.context:
**This dimension has concrete official mechanisms; it is not blank.**

The official docs call the framework a "data framework".

The core is structure your data (indices, graphs).
Plus a retrieval/query interface.

That is, "turn external data into retrievable context".

**How do retrieval results get packed into the context window?** The official answer is the Response Synthesizer:

- `compact` (default) — "stuff as many text ... that can fit within the context window"
- `refine` — refine chunk by chunk
- `tree_summarize` — recursive summarization
- `simple_summarize` — truncate to a single prompt

That is its context-trimming and summarization mechanism: pack to the window first, split into chunks when it does not fit, compress via the summarize-style modes.
axes.permissions:
**⚠ This is a clear, major information gap; confirm it yourself before choosing.**

**Things the official README never mentions**: sandboxing, a file-permission model,
network access controls, human-in-the-loop confirmation — not one.

Compared against the other orchestration frameworks this site files:

- Google ADK has Tool Confirmation (HITL)
- CrewAI has guardrails (mechanism undocumented)
- LangGraph has interrupts (state can be inspected and modified)
- **LlamaIndex — the README does not even name the concept**

⚠ **The nature of the risk surface is different.** Its main battleground is document parsing and RAG;
what it handles is usually **user-uploaded data**.

That is a different class of risk from "an agent touching your local files" (data-leakage surface vs host-operation surface).

But **the README does not discuss data permissions or isolation**.
axes.fit:
**A fit: bringing external data in for retrieval-augmented Q&A.**

- The core task is ingesting external data sources (APIs / PDFs / docs / SQL) for retrieval and Q&A
- You need one of the 300+ ready-made integrations
- The team is on the Python stack
- You explicitly want LlamaParse's parsing capabilities (that goes through the commercial platform)

**Not a fit in three situations.**

- You need an agent to read/write files in your own project directory and run commands — that is the Deep Agents class of "workspace file system"
- You need explicit sandboxing and permission boundaries — the official framework docs have no such mechanisms
- You need "hosted continuation after shutdown" — that goes through the LlamaAgents platform side

sections.两个安装档位：它少见的清晰之处:
**The two starting paths the README gives are clearer than many frameworks'.**

| Tier | Package | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Starter** | `llama-index` | Core plus a bundle of common integrations, for convenience |
| **Customized** | `llama-index-core` | Core only, then pick from the integrations page as needed |

**The namespace rule is worth remembering** (README code example):

```python
from llama_index.core.xxx import ClassABC      # with .core = core
from llama_index.xxx.yyy import SubclassABC    # without = an integration package
```

⚠ **One positioning gap**: the README has no CLI launch command, no Web UI, no container deployment example.

Compare with other objects filed in the same section:

- Google ADK — has `adk deploy docker` and `cloud_run`
- OpenHands — four deployment forms

**Conclusion: LlamaIndex is a library, not a platform.**
sections.300+ 集成：优势也是维护负担:
⚠ **The official wording is "work seamlessly."** This site has not measured cross-provider capability alignment for any of them.

When choosing, do not just check that a package name exists — also check that integration package's maintenance status and issues.
sections.最需要区分的一处：数据接入 ≠ agent 文件操作:
**This is the spot this site thinks is most easily misread.**

| Object | Capability | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| **LlamaIndex** | data connectors ingest APIs / PDFs / docs / SQL; parsing, indexing, retrieval | **Data-source layer** |
| **Deep Agents** | filesystem; the agent reads/writes files in a workspace | **Workspace layer** |

**Both get called "file-related", but they are completely different things.**

When choosing, first ask which one you need:

- "Turn a pile of documents into a retrievable knowledge base"
- "Let an agent work inside my project directory"

runs:
This site has not completed measured runs. The test protocol is at [protocols/framework/_protocol.md](../../../protocols/framework/_protocol.md).

**Suggested measurement** (tailored to the question "has the strategy really shifted"):

| # | What to test | Why it is worth testing |
|:--:|---|---|
| 1 | After installing llama-index-core, check the API shape and version of `llama_index.core.workflow` | The official docs already state it is still in core; measurement confirms the usable orchestration surface |
| 2 | Run a minimal "documents → retrieval Q&A" loop on the Starter tier | Judge whether its current core experience is smooth |
| 3 | Actual coverage of data ingestion (this time pick one PDF + one SQL) | "300+ integrations" and "API/PDF/docs/SQL" are different claims — test the concrete ones |
| 4 | Retrieval quality and structured output after switching to a non-OpenAI provider | The official page says work seamlessly; that needs verification |
| 5 | Context trimming of retrieval results on long documents (synthesis modes are officially documented) | Actual behaviour still awaits measurement |
| 6 | Compare LlamaIndex OSS vs LlamaParse in practice | The vendor itself says focus has shifted; how big the gap is needs a first-hand look |
